title: Batch jobs record their billed instance time
description:
Every cost number in this epic rests on one input: how many GPU-instance
seconds a Batch job actually consumed. We do not record it.

`duration_seconds` is `completed_at - claimed_at`, which measures our own
container's working time. It omits everything AWS bills before the container
claims anything: EC2 boot, ECS agent registration, and the GPU image pull.
With `minv_cpus=0` in the compute environment, every cold start pays that,
and on a cold start it can exceed the synthesis itself.

The Batch job ID is already available -- the runner claims as
`f"batch:{AWS_BATCH_JOB_ID}"` (`worker-image/src/runner.py:117`), so
`claimed_by` carries it. This story turns that into timing facts on the record.

## Feature

```gherkin
Feature: Recording billed instance time for Batch jobs

  Scenario: A completed Batch job records its AWS timings
    Given a Batch job has completed for a content hash
    When the Batch completion event is processed
    Then the job records the Batch created, started, and stopped times
    And the job records its instance type
    And the job records its billed seconds

  Scenario: Billed seconds include provisioning for a cold start
    Given a Batch job started on a newly provisioned instance
    When the Batch completion event is processed
    Then the billed seconds exceed the container runtime

  Scenario: A warm start is not charged for provisioning
    Given a Batch job started on an already running instance
    When the Batch completion event is processed
    Then the billed seconds equal the container runtime

  Scenario: A locally processed job records no billed instance time
    Given a job was claimed by a local worker
    When the job is marked done
    Then the job records no billed seconds

  Scenario: A failed Batch job still records its billed time
    Given a Batch job has failed for a content hash
    When the Batch completion event is processed
    Then the job records its billed seconds
```

A failed job burns GPU exactly like a successful one. Cost tracking that only
counts successes will understate spend precisely when things are going wrong.

## Implementation brief

**`cdk/stacks/backend.py`**

- EventBridge rule on `aws.batch`, detail-type `Batch Job State Change`, with
  `detail.status` in `["SUCCEEDED", "FAILED"]`, filtered to our job queue.
  Target a new `batch_telemetry` Lambda.
- Do NOT extend the router for this. It is event-driven, not request-driven,
  and the router is already carrying more than it should.
- Grant the new Lambda `batch:DescribeJobs` and read/write on the jobs table.

**`cdk/lambdas/batch_telemetry/handler.py`** (new)

- The event carries `detail.jobId`, `detail.createdAt`, `detail.startedAt`,
  `detail.stoppedAt`, `detail.container.instanceType` (confirm the exact
  shape against a real event -- do not trust this list).
- Map back to the job: query the jobs table for the record whose `claimed_by`
  equals `f"batch:{jobId}"`. **There is no index on `claimed_by`** -- either
  add a GSI, or pass the content hash through as a Batch container environment
  variable and read it off the event's container overrides. The second is
  cheaper and the Step Functions task already sets container overrides
  (`cdk/stacks/backend.py`, `submit_batch`); prefer it.
- `container_seconds = (stoppedAt - startedAt) / 1000`
- `provisioning_seconds`: when `startedAt - createdAt` exceeds a configurable
  warm-start threshold, the job triggered a scale-up; charge a configurable
  `provisioning_overhead_seconds`. Otherwise zero. Both values are CDK
  context settings, not literals.
- `billed_seconds = container_seconds + provisioning_seconds`
- Write `batch_created_at`, `batch_started_at`, `batch_stopped_at`,
  `instance_type`, `container_seconds`, `provisioning_seconds`,
  `billed_seconds` to the job record. Do not overwrite `duration_seconds`;
  it means something different and the console already shows it.

## Note on shared instances

Two concurrent jobs on one `g4dn.xlarge` each record full container seconds,
so their sum overstates true instance time. With `maxv_cpus=8` and a 4-vCPU
instance type the ceiling is two concurrent jobs, so the worst case is a
2x overstatement in a window where both run. Amortization is deliberately out
of scope here -- record the raw facts first. The reconciliation story will
reveal whether the overlap is frequent enough to be worth modelling.

## Acceptance

`make check` green, and a recorded Batch completion event fixture produces the
expected attributes.
